Restocking a Proven Shield

When Iranian ballistic missiles streaked toward Israel in 2024, two U.S. Navy destroyers, the USS Arleigh Burke and the USS Carney, answered with the SM-3. It was the first time the interceptor had ever been fired in combat, and it worked. Now the Pentagon is paying to make sure it never runs short of them.

This week, Raytheon announced a five-year contract worth $6.3 billion, with two more option years, to keep its production line turning out the Standard Missile-3 Block IB. The deal is aimed squarely at one problem: America has been firing expensive interceptors faster than it can build them.

The SM-3 is an unusual weapon. It carries no explosive warhead. Instead, it destroys an incoming ballistic missile by slamming into it at tremendous speed, a technique known as hit-to-kill, essentially stopping a bullet with another bullet. Launched from both ships and land, and guided by an infrared seeker, it is built to catch enemy missiles in the middle of their flight, high above the earth.

The urgency is real. A recent think-tank report listed the SM-3 among seven critical munitions, alongside the Patriot, THAAD, and the Tomahawk, that U.S. forces are burning through faster than the stockpile can handle. “It has proven its relevance in combat,” said Raytheon president Phil Jasper, describing the interceptor as central to protecting U.S. forces and allies.

Building a weapon that works is one thing. Making sure you have enough of it is another, and that is what this deal is really about.
